turns.en: Mike, welcome back to the long view. Thank you for having me. That's great to be back. Well, it's great to have you and I loved the book. I think it's the right book at the right time by the right person because this is a complicated topic and we're looking forward to delving into it

turns.en: with you today. Let's start with a really basic question. How do you define a cyber crime? That's a great question. So the word cyber crime, the only time I use it in my book is referring to some statistics from the FBI about increases in cyber crime. What's kind of funny to me is that
turns.zh: 我们今天就来好好聊聊。先从一个非常基础的问题开始：你怎么定义网络犯罪？——这个问题问得好。其实“网络犯罪”这个词，我在书里唯一一次用到，是在引用 FBI 关于网络犯罪增长的一些统计数据。有意思的是，

turns.zh: 在他们的报告里，FBI 自己其实并没有给出定义。他们只是举了一些例子，所以基本就是你预想的那些：网络钓鱼（phishing）犯罪、涉及恶意软件（malware）的犯罪、勒索软件（ransomware）等等。它不包括有人拿枪指着你说

turns.zh: “把钱包交出来”，但它涵盖了这类犯罪的各种电子化版本。

turns.en: In the book, you note that there was actually a 10-fold increase in cyber crime between 2018 and 2025. What were some of the main factors behind that huge increase? This is for victims age 60 and up and the number, it's an 11.9 times increase from 2018 to 2025,
turns.zh: 你在书里提到，2018 到 2025 年间，网络犯罪其实增长了 10 倍。这么大的增幅背后，主要有哪些原因？——这指的是 60 岁及以上的受害者，而且这个数字，从 2018 到 2025 年增长了 11.9 倍，

turns.en: which is absolutely mind-blowing. There's a lot of reasons for that. Number one, of course, is just an aging population. As we age, various changes can happen that can make us more vulnerable, whether those are cognitive changes or life circumstances changes. Another big part of it
turns.zh: 这简直令人难以置信。原因有很多。第一个，当然是人口老龄化。随着我们变老，会发生各种变化，让我们更容易受到侵害，无论是认知方面的变化，还是生活状况方面的变化。另一个重要原因是，

turns.en: is that just in the last handful of years, the tools that the bad guys have, essentially, have become much stronger as AI capabilities have improved dramatically. While that's happening, while their tools are becoming much stronger, the truth is that most individuals, especially older
turns.zh: 就在最近这几年，随着人工智能（AI）能力的大幅提升，坏人手中的工具本质上已经变得强大得多。而在这同时——他们的工具越来越强的同时——事实是，大多数人，尤其是年长的

turns.en: individuals, their own security practices aren't really any different than they were a handful of years ago. So when you have one side getting a lot more powerful and the other side basically continuing to do the same thing, there's been a big shift in the balance of power, essentially.
turns.zh: 人，他们自己的安全防护做法其实和几年前没什么两样。所以当一方变得强大得多，另一方却基本还是老样子，力量对比本质上已经发生了巨大的转变。

turns.en: So we want to delve into aging and cognitive decline as a dimension of this. We'll cover that later. But let's stick with AI for a moment, Mike, because you note that the increasing sophistication of AI is a big factor here. So what types of AI-related scams and frauds have you been seeing
turns.zh: 我们想深入聊聊老龄化和认知衰退这个话题，它是其中一个维度，我们稍后会谈到。不过 Mike，我们先在 AI 这里停一下，因为你提到 AI 日益复杂化是这里的一个大因素。那你都见到过哪些与 AI 相关的骗局和欺诈，

turns.en: and you're most concerned about? Yeah, there's a ton. And in many ways, it's really
turns.zh: 又是你最担心的那些？——嗯，太多了。而且从很多方面看，这其实就是

turns.en: AI making it a lot easier and faster to do the same types of frauds that people have always been doing. One example, before it might have been very easy to look at a fake email that's pretending to be from your bank and quickly identify that there's a whole bunch of typos and misspellings
turns.zh: AI 让人们一直以来搞的那些欺诈套路，变得更容易、更快速地实施。举个例子，以前你看到一封假装是你银行发来的假邮件，很容易就能一眼发现里面有一大堆错别字、拼写错误

turns.en: at grammatical errors in it, whereas now using an AI chatbot, it's very easy for somebody who doesn't even know English at all to write a convincingly worded and an email of perfect grammar in English. So something as simple as that. But there's also the fact that it's much easier, much less expensive
turns.zh: 和语法错误；而现在，借助 AI 聊天机器人，一个完全不懂英语的人，也能轻轻松松写出一封措辞可信、语法完美的英文邮件。就是这么简单的一件事。但还有一点，就是对坏人来说，如今搞出非常有针对性的攻击，要容易得多、也便宜得多，

turns.en: for the bad guys to create very targeted attacks now than it used to be, because you can automate research. You can ask an AI bot to research an individual person, find everything they've posted on social media, find anything that other people have posted on social media, look at obituaries,
turns.zh: 因为你可以把调研工作自动化。你可以让一个 AI 机器人去调查某个具体的人，找出这个人在社交媒体上发过的所有内容，找出别人在社交媒体上发过的关于他的任何信息，翻看讣告，

turns.en: look at whatever articles you can find, and craft a very highly targeted attack. And before that used to be an extremely manual labor intensive process, so something like that would have been reserved only for very high value targets, whereas now you can automate that at a very low cost and
turns.zh: 查阅你能找到的任何文章，然后炮制出一个针对性极强的攻击。而在以前，这是一个极其依赖人工、极其耗力的过程，所以这种做法只会留给价值非常高的目标；可现在你能以极低的成本把它自动化，

turns.en: deploy that type of attack against all sorts of people at a broad scale. Just to give one example, Christine, you might personally find this interesting because you're involved actually. Not long ago, I asked the particular AI, it knows who I am already, and it knows I've been
turns.zh: 并大规模地对形形色色的人发动这类攻击。就举一个例子吧——Christine，你个人可能会觉得这个很有意思，因为里面其实牵扯到了你。不久前，我问了某个特定的 AI——它已经知道我是谁，也知道我一直在

turns.en: writing about cyber security, and so I asked it, create a profile of me as if you were going to plan an attack against me, and what would you do? And it thought for a couple of minutes, and it came back, and it shared all sorts of information about me. And of course, my job is fairly public,
turns.zh: 写网络安全方面的内容，所以我就问它：假设你要策划一场针对我的攻击，请给我建一份画像，你会怎么做？它思考了几分钟，然后回来，分享了一大堆关于我的信息。当然，我的工作算是比较公开的，

turns.en: so a lot of this is pretty easy to find. But it also found some things that I've never written about. And so I guess perhaps another family member shared it on social media or some things that was interesting. But then here's the most interesting part. It said, if I were to craft an attack
turns.zh: 所以这里面很多东西都很容易查到。但它还找到了一些我从没写过的东西。所以我猜，也许是家里其他人在社交媒体上分享过，反正就是有些挺有意思的东西。但接下来才是最有意思的部分。它说，如果我要策划一场

turns.en: against you, I would probably impersonate Jim Dolly, Christine Benz, or John Luskin, because those are people who I know that you have known for a long time, you trust them, and you consider to them to be friends. So if they asked you to do a favor, you would be inclined to do it. Plus,
turns.zh: 针对你的攻击，我大概会冒充 Jim Dolly、Christine Benz 或 John Luskin，因为我知道这几个人是你认识很久的、你信任的、被你当作朋友的人。所以如果他们请你帮个忙，你会倾向于答应。再加上，

turns.en: all three of those people have, there's lots of public record of the three of you speaking and talking, so it would be easy to mimic you to create a deep-faked video or voice message impersonating you. But when I saw that, it was just, wow, because that's exactly right. I do consider the three
turns.zh: 这三个人的公开资料都很多——你们几个公开发言、对谈的记录一大堆，所以很容易模仿、做出冒充他们的深度伪造（deepfake）视频或语音消息。但我看到这段的时候，只觉得，哇，因为说得完全没错。我确实把这

turns.en: of you to be friends, and I would be likely to do, you know, and want to do a favor for you if you ask. It's so on the mark, and I know a lot of people might say, oh, my life isn't as public. I don't post things on social media, and that's good, but sometimes the attack won't be that,
turns.zh: 三个人当作朋友，如果你们开口，我也很可能会、也乐意帮这个忙。它说得太准了。我知道很多人可能会说：哦，我的生活没那么公开，我不在社交媒体上发东西。这很好，但有时候攻击的切入点并不是你本人，

turns.en: it will be, they researched your granddaughter who does post everything on social media, and they don't actually need to know very much about you, because the attack is convincingly mimicking your granddaughter, and they have lots of material to use for that, and that's how they come after you.
turns.zh: 而是——他们去调查了你的孙女，她在社交媒体上什么都发。他们其实不需要太了解你本人，因为这场攻击是逼真地模仿你的孙女，而且他们手上有大量素材可以用来模仿，他们就是这样冲你来的。

turns.en: So it's just much easier now for very targeted attacks to be created at a low cost.
turns.zh: 所以现在，以低成本炮制出针对性极强的攻击，简直太容易了。

turns.en: That's pretty scary. One of your pieces of advice is that you have to know your opponent when it comes to these cybercriminals, why is that important, and what should we know about them? Yeah, the message there that I'm trying to get across is that these are professionals,
turns.zh: 这挺吓人的。你有一条建议是：面对这些网络罪犯，你必须了解你的对手。为什么这一点很重要？我们应该了解他们些什么？——嗯，我想传达的信息是：这些人都是职业选手，

turns.en: right? Like when you think of yourself and the people you work with, you've had this career for however many years, and you've spent all this time building up your skills and learning technologies, and that's what these people are doing, too. This is their career, and they probably
turns.zh: 对吧？就像你想想你自己和你的同事，你们干这行多少年了，花了这么多时间打磨技能、学习技术——这些人干的也是一样的事。这就是他们的职业，而且他们很可能

turns.en: work as a team with other skilled professionals, each with their own areas of expertise, and so you're working against skilled professionals with very powerful tools. It's important to recognize that that is who the bad guy is in this case. So there are so many different varieties of fraud
turns.zh: 是和其他技术娴熟的专业人士组成团队作案，每个人各有专长。所以你对抗的是手握强大工具的专业人士。认清这一点很重要——在这件事里，坏人就是这样的存在。而欺诈的花样实在太多，

turns.en: that it's difficult to keep track. In fact, I liked your caution in the book where you're like, don't even try to memorize all these things because they're changing so quickly, they're proliferating, but you note in the book that there are some commonalities in these cyber frauds often follow
turns.zh: 多到让人应接不暇。其实我很喜欢你书里的那个提醒，你说，别想着把这些全都记住，因为它们变化太快、还在不断增多。但你在书里也指出，这些网络欺诈有一些共通之处，往往遵循

turns.en: a two-step process. Can you talk about that? Yeah, almost every fraud is going to have to do two things. The first step is they have to get your trust in some way, and sometimes that's very quick. It's just an email that appears to be from your brokerage firm, and it was good enough that it
turns.zh: 一个两步走的套路。你能讲讲吗？——嗯，几乎每一种欺诈都得做两件事。第一步，他们必须设法取得你的信任，有时候这一步非常快。就是一封看起来像是你券商发来的邮件，做得足够逼真，

turns.en: convinced you, for instance, so they got your trust in just seconds. Other times, it could be a longer bar drawn out affair, where it's a message from someone you don't know over social media, and they build what feels like a real relationship with you over time when, in reality,
turns.zh: 比如说，把你骗信了，于是他们几秒钟内就取得了你的信任。另一些时候，这可能是个更漫长、更拖沓的过程：对方通过社交媒体给你发消息，是个你不认识的人，随着时间推移，他们和你建立起一种看似真实的关系，可实际上，

turns.en: right from the start, they're just, this is all step one of a fraud. They're just trying to build trust with you over time. So that's the first step is gaining your trust somehow. And the second step is that now that I've got your trust, there's going to be some call to action,
turns.zh: 从一开始，这一切就是欺诈的第一步而已。他们只是想慢慢和你建立信任。所以第一步就是设法取得你的信任。而第二步是：既然我已经取得了你的信任，接下来就会有某个“行动号召”，

turns.en: and that could be any number of different things. I think it's useful to group those into kind of two categories. The first category is things that will give them access to your account in some way. So that would be phishing, you know, if they're asking you to share your login credentials to
turns.zh: 而这个行动号召可能是各种各样的东西。我觉得把它们大致分成两类会很有用。第一类，是那些能让他们以某种方式拿到你账户访问权限的东西。比如说网络钓鱼——如果他们要你分享某个账户的登录凭证（login credentials），

turns.en: something or share a multifactor authentication code or anything that involves you end up with malware on your device so that they can harvest your login credentials, so things like that. And the second category of call to action is things that don't end up in them having access to
turns.zh: 或者要你分享一个多因素认证（multi-factor authentication）验证码，或者任何会导致你设备上被植入恶意软件、从而让他们能够窃取你登录凭证的情况，诸如此类。第二类行动号召，则是那些最终不会让他们拿到

turns.en: your account, but rather you essentially just paying the money directly because you thought they were somebody else. Things included in that category, a lot of times frauds will involve asking for payment by gift card or by cryptocurrency. Either one of those is a huge red flag. If you ever
turns.zh: 你账户访问权限的东西，而本质上是你因为以为对方是别人，就直接把钱付了出去。这一类里包括的东西——很多欺诈会要求你用礼品卡或加密货币（cryptocurrency）付款。这两种付款方式中的任何一种，都是一个巨大的危险信号。如果你曾经

turns.en: encounter requests of that nature, assume it's fraud and so proven otherwise because the reason that those are so preferred as means of payment by thieves is that they are very hard to track and very hard payments to reverse. So it's helpful to kind of think about the two steps gaining your
turns.zh: 遇到这类要求，就先假定它是欺诈，除非有证据证明不是。因为窃贼之所以这么偏爱这两种付款方式，正是因为它们极难追踪、付款也极难撤销。所以，把这两步——取得你的

turns.en: trust and these calls to action because we want to put roadblocks in place for each of those two different steps basically. You also note that as an overall policy, everyone should be skeptical about any type of incoming communications, email, text, etc. about your financial accounts.
turns.zh: 信任和这些行动号召——放在一起想是很有用的，因为基本上我们要针对这两个不同的步骤分别设置障碍。你还提到，作为一个总体原则，每个人都应该对任何主动找上门来的、涉及你财务账户的通信保持警惕，不管是邮件、短信等等。

turns.en: What should people do instead? Yes, exactly. So this is the two steps that we were just talking about. The first step is to gain your trust somehow and that's going to be through some sort of incoming communication and so we need to be very skeptical of them. That plays out in a number of
turns.zh: 那人们应该怎么做呢？——对，正是如此。这就是我们刚才说的那两步。第一步是设法取得你的信任，而这会通过某种主动找上门的通信来实现，所以我们需要对它们非常警惕。具体体现在很多

turns.en: different ways. Number one, we don't want to click links and emails. We don't want to be following QR codes. Also, replying is not something we want to do. If it's an incoming phone call, if it's from a number that we don't know, just let it go to voicemail rather than answering it.
turns.zh: 不同的方面。第一，我们不要点邮件里的链接。我们不要去扫二维码（QR code）。还有，我们也不要去回复。如果是打进来的电话，只要号码是我们不认识的，就让它转到语音信箱，别接。

turns.zh: 信息、并提出那些重要的话题。而且坦白说，我觉得我们需要在这方面再加强一点。所以看到 Dana 提出这个话题、看到你们三个人一起讨论它，我真是太高兴了。——另一个重要议题，是网络犯罪和

turns.zh: 先等着，等我们知道情况好像有点不对劲了，再去落实保护措施。但我们现在能看到——已经有相关研究表明，财务问题本身就是那个早期预警信号。所以，一直等到还有别的东西

turns.en: obviously wrong, you know, waiting until, you know, you can tell, just from talking to mom or dad or whoever, that that something is off by the time you see that, there's potentially been financial problems for years on average for six years. And so to me, the ramifications there
turns.zh: 明显不对劲了才行动——你知道，一直等到你光凭和妈妈、爸爸或某个人聊几句就能听出“有点不对劲”的时候——等你看出这一点时，财务问题可能已经持续好几年了，平均而言长达六年。所以在我看来，这其中的影响，

turns.en: until we see it. Because by then it's too late. The damage is, or at least the significant part of the damage has already occurred. Right. So to follow up on that, Mike, how can people be preemptive? Like you're saying sort of assume the worst, assume that you may have cognitive decline.
turns.zh: 真的看到了才行动，因为到那时就太晚了。损害——或者说至少是损害中相当大的一部分——已经发生了。——好。那么顺着这一点追问一下，Mike，人们要怎么做到防患于未然？就像你说的，有点往最坏处假设，假设你自己可能会出现认知衰退，

turns.en: And that might diminish your judgment. So how can people get in front of that potential issue and protect themselves? Yeah, I think one of the things we've already talked about on the cyber security front is Pascis, also physical security keys, like ubiquies, because again,
turns.zh: 而这可能会削弱你的判断力。那么人们要怎样抢在这个潜在问题前面、保护好自己呢？——嗯，我觉得我们已经谈到的其中一点，就是在网络安全方面用通行密钥，还有像 YubiKey 那样的实体安全密钥，因为再说一次，

turns.zh: 它们能抵抗网络钓鱼。因为随着认知衰退而下降的能力之一，就是我们察觉“可疑、像是钓鱼”的敏感度，所以我们更容易被骗。因此，如果你用的东西是钓不动的——通行密钥基本上就钓不动——你就会更安全。

turns.zh: 但更广泛地说，我觉得其中一件重要的事，是建立某种监督机制。我知道很多家庭——对已婚夫妻来说——他们已经在这么做了：每个月两人一起过一遍自己的开销，或者投资

turns.zh: 账户之类的，把每一样都看一遍。这个做法的核心是：我们希望有两个自认为头脑清醒的人，能够一起看信用卡账单，并确认账单上的每一笔都是本该在那儿的。

turns.en: And then same thing with the bank statement, the checking accounts. And then same thing with the investment accounts, we want to be able to have two people who we think are both of sound and mind looking at this. And you know, if any big changes were made, any big transactions or
turns.zh: 银行对账单、支票账户也是同样的道理。投资账户也一样——我们希望能有两个我们都认为头脑清醒的人一起来看这些。而且，如果有任何大的变动、任何大额交易，或者

turns.zh: 有任何钱从账户里被转走，我们都想知道为什么。我们希望能有把握地确认：是的，这件事的发生是有原因的，我们知道那是什么原因，而且是有意的。所以在某个时点，对于没有结婚的人，或者对于任何

turns.zh: 可能是成年的子女，可能是侄女或外甥，或者对一些人来说，得是一位金融专业人士。如果你家里没有一个人恰好具备这些技能、或有时间等等，如果你身边没有一位能够
